rule: A value in this file is a product, security or SLO choice the implementation must NOT invent. Each entry records the safe default in force, why that default is safe rather than correct, and what an owner decision would change. An entry stays OPEN until an owner records a decision; while OPEN, no gate may be claimed on the strength of the default.

entries.title: Soak duration and long-run thresholds
entries.question: How long is the release soak, and what are its pass thresholds?
entries.default_in_force: None. No soak is claimed anywhere in this repository.
entries.why_safe: Claiming a soak that was not run is the failure mode; claiming none is merely incomplete. G12 names the long release soak; anything shorter is reconnaissance and is labelled as such.
entries.owner_decision_changes: The G12 gate definition and the evidence schema for soak runs.

entries.title: Snapshot-admission watermark wait deadline
entries.question: How long may snapshot admission wait for the visibility watermark before the database is declared unavailable?
entries.default_in_force: 600 seconds, then fail-stop with diagnostics naming the target and current watermark (fork/typedb/storage/storage.rs, WATERMARK_WAIT_DEADLINE).
entries.why_safe: The previous behaviour was an unbounded spin: an unresolved commit obligation presented as every later snapshot open hanging with no diagnostic. Any finite bound is safer than none, and 600s is far beyond any healthy wait, so the bound fires only when a slot is genuinely stuck. It is deliberately NOT tuned for throughput.
entries.owner_decision_changes: The value, and whether the terminal action is a fail-stop or a typed unavailable response (the latter requires changing open_snapshot_* to fallible signatures across the concept/database/query layers).

entries.title: Data-path object size ceiling
entries.question: What is the maximum single data-path object the control plane admits?
entries.default_in_force: 8 MiB (control-plane/src/controller/core/capability.ts MAX_CAPABILITY_BYTES, worker-entry.ts MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES), enforced before the body is read and again after.
entries.why_safe: It is the figure the F9 contract clause names, and it is enforced as a CEILING that a capability may narrow but never widen - so an over-permissive issuer cannot raise it.
entries.owner_decision_changes: The ceiling, and whether oversized payloads get a chunked/streamed path instead of a refusal.

entries.title: Concurrent R2 subrequests per worker invocation
entries.question: How many concurrent R2 reads may one invocation issue?
entries.default_in_force: 6 (control-plane/src/controller/worker-entry.ts R2_SUBREQUEST_CEILING), taken from the Cloudflare contract lock's 'simultaneous outgoing connections per invocation is six'.
entries.why_safe: It is the platform's stated hard ceiling rather than a tuned number; the previous value of 8 was a request the platform cannot serve. Reserving headroom below 6 for control connections is a plausible refinement, but lowering it is a performance decision, not a safety one.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Whether to reserve headroom below the platform ceiling, and how the reservation is accounted when a route makes both DO and R2 calls.

entries.title: Flake-ledger expiry policy
entries.question: How long may a tolerated anomaly stay in docs/evidence/flake-ledger.json before it must be fixed or re-justified?
entries.default_in_force: Per-entry expiry dates, currently 2027-06-30 for the two live entries; an expired entry is reported and stops tolerating, it does not silently keep excluding.
entries.why_safe: Both live entries are upstream defects (todo!() stubs and a declared #[ignore]) that fail identically on the RocksDB oracle, so they are baseline-equal rather than port debt. The dates are placeholders chosen to be finite.
entries.owner_decision_changes: The maximum permitted exclusion lifetime and who may extend one.

entries.title: Storage async-bridge deadline and object-store retry bound
entries.question: How long may a single storage operation wait on the async->sync bridge before fail-stop, and how many times may SlateDB retry a failing object-store call?
entries.default_in_force: Bridge: report every 30 s (ERROR log naming the pending operation), abort the process at 600 s (fork/typedb/storage/keyspace/slate.rs, bridge()). Object store: object_store_max_retries = Some(8) in SlateKeyspace::settings(), replacing the upstream unbounded default.
entries.why_safe: The previous behaviour was an unbounded recv() over an unbounded retry loop: a persistent R2/S3 fault presented as a silent forever-hang holding storage locks. Fail-stop with a named operation is the same doctrine as Q-01's guard, and 600 s / 8 retries are far beyond any healthy operation, so the bounds fire only on genuine faults. Neither value is tuned for availability.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Both values, the report cadence, and whether the terminal action stays a process abort or becomes a typed storage-unavailable error surfaced through fallible read/write signatures.

entries.title: No-compactor lane L0 admission envelope
entries.question: With compaction and GC deliberately disabled (the pre-G13 containment posture), what is the maximum L0 SST count the remote/experimental lane may accumulate before it must refuse NEW writes with a typed error rather than degrade without bound?
entries.default_in_force: EXPERIMENTAL_NO_COMPACTOR_MAX_L0_SSTS = 50_000 (fork/typedb/storage/keyspace/slate.rs). At or above this observed L0 SST count (read from the in-memory manifest), put/write refuse with a typed ErrorKind::Invalid admission error; below it they succeed. SlateDB's own backpressure ceiling (settings.l0_max_ssts) is kept far higher so the TypeDB admission bound, not an opaque memtable stall, is what fires first.
entries.why_safe: A no-compactor lane whose L0 only ever grows will otherwise accumulate SSTs, read amplification, LIST/GET cost, memory and recovery time without any ceiling (S-05). The bound converts that unbounded degradation into an explicit, typed, non-transient refusal a caller/controller can observe and act on. 50_000 is a containment default chosen far above any healthy short-lived workload while still bounding the envelope; it is NOT a ratified capacity SLO.
entries.owner_decision_changes: The exact ceiling, whether the envelope is expressed as L0 SST count and/or total object count and/or total bytes, and whether reaching it triggers a controller-authorized fenced compaction instead of a hard write refusal.

entries.title: Confidentiality profile (v16 §19.6)
entries.question: Is provider-managed confidentiality (Profile P: TLS everywhere, R2 managed at-rest encryption, private service bindings, opaque keys, encrypted secret storage) sufficient, or must the application envelope-encrypt WAL bodies, prepared results and checkpoint/data objects before R2 (Profile E: vetted AEAD, per-database/per-generation DEK wrapped by a KMS/HSM KEK, associated data binding environment/tenant/database/generation/materialisation/key/type/format-version, independent backup keys)?
entries.default_in_force: NONE DECIDED (round-4 R4-SEC-02). Current controls are integrity-only: content SHA-256, authenticated journal entries, HMAC-signed capabilities. Nothing in this repository encrypts WAL payloads, result bytes, checkpoints or local S3 blobs at the application layer, and no gate may treat §19.6 as closed.
entries.why_safe: Refusing to guess is the safe default: silently choosing Profile P would bake in the assumption that Cloudflare-managed keys and plaintext-capable runtime principals satisfy the product's regulatory envelope; silently choosing Profile E would change caching, deduplication, checksums, recovery and performance without a measured decision. Both are owner calls (threat model + compliance), not implementation defaults.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Which encryption acceptance matrix (§5.4 of the round-4 directive) becomes mandatory; the key hierarchy (distinct capability-signing / journal-MAC / data-encryption / bootstrap roots, kid + rotation overlap); the backup-key administration boundary; and whether local caches/temp/checkpoint files require wipe policies.

entries.title: Local native S3 provider: RustFS strategic target, MinIO transition baseline
entries.question: Which native S3 server backs the local TypeDB/SlateDB object_store lane, given that the locked MinIO community binary (RELEASE.2025-09-07) is archived upstream and in the affected range of CVE-2026-41145 / GHSA-hv4r-mvr4-25vw with no patched community release?
entries.default_in_force: MinIO stays ONLY as a loopback-confined transition baseline (random per-run credentials, synthetic data, never exposed beyond 127.0.0.1). RustFS 1.0.0-rc.2 (signed release commit e9f5318, Apache-2.0, active security line, CAS-eligible write-path architecture) is the strategic replacement target. The default does NOT flip until one exact RustFS platform digest passes the full provider-neutral certification corpus (round-4 §6.4: SigV4, If-None-Match:* two-writer race with exactly one winner, If-Match update, timeout/ambiguity, multipart lifecycle, list pagination, crash/restart, the patched SlateDB suite and TypeDB corpus) plus readiness-by-authenticated-S3-operation. Versity v1.7.0 is REJECTED as a qualifying backend (dynamically reproduced conditional-create race: twelve concurrent If-None-Match:* PUTs all returned 200); Garage is rejected by its own documentation (conditional writes structurally unsupported).
entries.why_safe: Neither keeping a known-vulnerable unmaintained binary indefinitely nor flipping to an uncertified pre-GA server is safe; the recorded direction bounds MinIO's exposure (loopback, ephemeral credentials, synthetic data) while making promotion strictly conditional on executed semantics, not vendor claims.
entries.owner_decision_changes: If RustFS fails a mandatory semantic: either an upstream fix is awaited or the owner explicitly signs a time-bounded MinIO security-fork/waiver. Passing the gate makes RustFS the ordinary native-fidelity default and removes MinIO from the supported path.
entries.progress_2026_08_19: RustFS 1.0.0-rc.2 is now PINNED (source-lock node RUSTFS: release-zip sha256 dbe7b718…, binary sha256 d286e5f8…, tag commit e9f53180 verified against both git ls-remote and the binary's own --version attestation). Against exactly that binary, tools/s3-cert-corpus PASSED on 2026-08-19: SigV4 auth, byte-exact put/get/head, ranged reads, If-None-Match:* two-writer race with exactly one winner, If-Match update fencing, list pagination, multipart complete/abort, and kill -9 crash/restart byte-exact persistence — via object_store =0.14.1, the exact crate the storage engine uses. STILL OUTSTANDING before the default may flip: the timeout/ambiguity lane (fault-proxy schedules), the patched SlateDB suite, and the TypeDB corpus run on a RustFS backend. The corpus runner hard-refuses any rustfs binary whose digest differs from the lock. ROUND-5 HARDENING (R5-LOCAL-01/03): the CAS gate can no longer accidentally serialize — 100 barrier-released rounds x 16 independent-client writers with 1 MiB pairwise-distinct bodies, 50 current-ETag update-race rounds with post-race ABA refusal, and 20 rounds of 8 independent OS PROCESSES racing conditional create (start-file barrier, winner self-verifies byte-exact stored bytes). RustFS 1.0.0-rc.2 PASSED all of it on 2026-08-19, as did the MinIO baseline; each run now emits a SEALED evidence bundle (provider binary digest, per-phase logs+digests, crash receipt, root seal) verified by an independent verifier. Outstanding before the default flips: the timeout/ambiguity fault-proxy lane, the patched SlateDB suite and the TypeDB corpus on a RustFS backend.

entries.title: Qualification scope for the storage-adapter change: single-node semantic parity
entries.question: Do the official-driver cluster suites, which require a 3-node replicated TypeDB deployment, block the qualification claim for the SlateDB/object-store storage adapter?
entries.decision: NO. The change under qualification is the storage adapter (TypeDB storage -> SlateDB -> S3/R2 object store). The claim being made is SEMANTIC PARITY: that running TypeDB on the object-store backend produces the same behaviour as running it on the classic backend. That claim is fully exercised by a single-node server with object storage, which is what the driver lanes run. The cluster suites exercise multi-node replication and high availability, in which the storage adapter does not participate; they are therefore OUT OF SCOPE for this claim, recorded as a declared exclusion with this rationale, and NOT a precondition that keeps a row partial.
entries.default_in_force: Before this decision the cluster suites were treated as an unmet precondition, which held all six official-driver rows at PARTIAL for a reason unrelated to the property being qualified.
entries.why_safe: The exclusion is declared, scoped and reversible, not silent: the cluster suites are still enumerated, still reported as not executed, and would immediately re-enter scope for any claim about replication, failover or high availability. Nothing about this decision lets a scenario that DID run report a different outcome, and no cluster capability may be claimed anywhere on the strength of it.
entries.owner_decision_changes: tools/drivers/row_status.py classifies the cluster suites as out-of-scope rather than blocking, so a row whose only unmet suite is cluster is COVERED for the single-node semantic-parity claim.
does_not_authorise: any claim of clustered, replicated or highly-available operation
any claim that the storage adapter behaves correctly under multi-node epoch contention, which remains untested

entries.title: Lint scope for an overlay workspace: gate the fork's own files, not upstream's
entries.question: fork/typedb is 778 files, of which 742 are byte-identical to the pinned upstream revision. Should the Rust production lint gates apply to all of them, or only to the 36 the fork actually modifies?
entries.decision: ONLY THE FILES THE FORK MODIFIES. Ownership is DERIVED per file, never declared: a file is ours when its git blob id differs from the pinned upstream revision, or when upstream has no such file. Measured 2026-08-21, gating everything meant 1210 of 1287 clippy findings were about code nobody here wrote or may change, and the gate aborted on resource/profile.rs, a file identical to upstream.
entries.default_in_force: Before this decision rust.clippy ran with -D warnings over the whole overlay workspace and could not pass, which blocked the entire quality programme.
entries.why_safe: The rule is derived rather than listed, so there is nothing to keep in sync and no allowlist to rot; reverting a fork file to upstream's bytes correctly stops gating it, because it is upstream's code again. It cannot silently widen: if ownership cannot be derived (sources/ not materialised) the gate REFUSES rather than gating everything or nothing. Plain rustc warnings in owned files still count, so scoping by file does not quietly stop denying what -D warnings denied. The rejected alternative, fixing upstream's findings, would grow the fork patch set from 36 paths to hundreds and invalidate fork_staging.staged_tree_sha256, the identity every sealed evidence bundle binds.
entries.owner_decision_changes: .quality/policy.toml, xtask/src/quality/forkowned.rs, and the rust.clippy command shape for overlay workspaces.

entries.title: The one clippy error inside the quality controller itself
entries.question: xtask/src/quality/exec.rs carried clippy::manual_range_contains inside a #[cfg(test)] assertion. xtask/** is protected; may an implementation task fix it?
entries.decision: YES, as its own reviewed change. Approved 2026-08-21. The change is exactly equivalent for every f64 including NaN, since Range::contains is defined as start <= x && x < end. It weakens nothing, allows no lint and moves no threshold.
entries.default_in_force: rust.clippy was red on the controller's own source, and this was almost certainly clippy's first execution against this repository: round 6's disk floor refused every compiling gate.
entries.why_safe: The finding was re-confirmed under the PINNED toolchain before being acted on. It first appeared under ambient clippy 1.94.0 while .prototools pins 1.93.0; after `rustup override set 1.93.0`, clippy 0.1.93 emits the same lint. Acting on a lint the pinned compiler does not emit would have been a change with no cause.
entries.owner_decision_changes: xtask/src/quality/exec.rs only.

entries.title: ENOSPC is an infrastructure failure, and the disk floor is per gate and workspace
entries.question: A gate that dies on 'No space left on device' was reported as a QualityFailure, and a single cost-class disk floor admitted a build it could not finish. Fix both?
entries.decision: BOTH. ENOSPC is typed InfrastructureFailure with a `cargo clean` remediation. Floors are keyed '<gate>@<manifest>' falling back to '<manifest>' falling back to the cost class, checked immediately before the command that builds that workspace, and an override may only RAISE the class floor.
entries.default_in_force: 14 GB free passed the 12 GB heavy floor; the build then consumed 23 GB without finishing and the run reported '0 infrastructure failure(s)'.
entries.why_safe: AGENTS.md 3.7 insists an infrastructure failure is never a pass; the converse matters as much, because a QualityFailure sends the next reader hunting for a defect in code that compiles fine. The floor for rust.tests@fork/typedb/Cargo.toml is 30 GB, and the policy comment records that 23 GB is a MEASURED LOWER BOUND rather than a proven sufficient figure, so it can be raised on evidence; with ENOSPC now typed correctly, being wrong fails safe. The key is per gate because clippy type-checks the same workspace in 4.5 GB while nextest links every test binary.
entries.owner_decision_changes: .quality/policy.toml [execution], xtask/src/quality/{exec,gates,policy}.rs.

entries.title: A PRISTINE bundle must list its unstaged fork patches
entries.question: Mutants 6/6b relabel a tree as PRISTINE. Against a genuinely pristine bundle the only field that actually changed was unstaged_fork_patches (36 entries -> []), which verify_leaf.py did not check, so the forgery went undetected. Close it?
entries.decision: YES. verify_leaf.py refuses a PRISTINE claim that lists no unstaged fork patches: pristine means the fork is NOT staged, so its patches must all appear unstaged, and an empty list is self-contradictory.
entries.default_in_force: The U0 lane had no internal defence against being relabelled at all; leaf_mutants reported 14/16 against u0-full-1.
entries.why_safe: It closes a real forgery rather than suppressing its report, and it narrows an ASSERTED LIMIT rather than deleting it. Control 6c previously asserted that the forgery is undetectable from inside the bundle; that is no longer true, so 6c was RESTATED and made source-state aware instead of removed for being inconvenient. The surviving limit is stated exactly: against a PRISTINE source bundle a forger who also leaves the fork-patch list intact still gets through, and only --corroborate-tree refuses it.
entries.owner_decision_changes: tools/qualification/verify_leaf.py and the 6/6b/6c controls in tools/qualification/leaf_mutants.py.

entries.title: Runtime output does not make a pristine tree dirty
entries.question: executed_tree_identity() decided PRISTINE from raw `git status`, which counts the typedb-logs/ directory a run writes into the checkout. Since a U0 run necessarily writes it, a U0 bundle could never be corroborated on the machine that produced it. Fix it?
entries.decision: YES. PRISTINE is decided on the SOURCE delta — the same set staged_delta_sha256 is computed over, which already excludes RUNTIME_OUTPUT and NON_CARGO_INPUT. verify_leaf.py's PRISTINE branch correspondingly refuses diverging SOURCE paths while tolerating runtime output.
entries.default_in_force: The workaround was to delete sources/typedb/typedb-logs before every U0 run, which is a manual step nobody will remember.
entries.why_safe: The implementation now matches its own docstring, which already named this exact case. `dirty` keeps its old meaning (raw git status nonempty) so the two producers cannot be read as disagreeing, and the path stays listed by name in runtime_output_paths, so nothing is hidden. Regression-checked: leaf_mutants still 16/16 against u1-full-1, and all four sealed bundles still verify CLEAN.
entries.owner_decision_changes: tools/qualification/leaf_common.py and tools/qualification/verify_leaf.py.

entries.title: A mutant that mutates nothing is not a survivor
entries.question: A control whose mutation leaves the bundle unchanged reported SURVIVED, which is indistinguishable from a real check having regressed. Report it differently?
entries.decision: YES. Every mutating control asserts its mutation actually landed, comparing the bundle by meaning; one that changes nothing reports N/A and counts as neither a kill nor a survival.
entries.default_in_force: Ambiguous SURVIVED lines, and the same class of false report in tools/release/release_mutants.py when a build artifact is absent.
entries.why_safe: The probe covers EVERY file in the bundle: each .json parsed (refresh() re-serialises, so raw bytes always differ) and every other file by digest, plus the name list so a deletion registers. An earlier attempt snapshotted only the results file and the logs and silently disabled control 10, which mutates only the COMPLETE marker; that attempt was REVERTED rather than shipped, and the replacement is regression-tested against exactly that failure — 16 controls RUN against both u1-full-1 and u0-full-1.
entries.owner_decision_changes: tools/qualification/leaf_mutants.py. tools/release/release_mutants.py carries the same defect and is NOT yet fixed.

entries.title: Should rust.tests cover an overlay workspace whose corpus is certified by the lane runners?
entries.question: `rust.tests` runs `cargo nextest run --manifest-path fork/typedb/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features`. That parallelises a test corpus upstream wrote assuming one server at a time, and manufactures failures that do not exist. Should the gate cover this workspace at all, and if so under what execution model?
entries.resolution: The question is withdrawn because its premise no longer holds. It asked which coverage or wall-clock the repository should GIVE UP to stop a parallel runner manufacturing failures. A fourth answer gives up neither: every test binary is invoked through tools/dev/netns_exec.py, which puts it in its OWN network namespace (unshare(CLONE_NEWNET), loopback brought up via SIOCSIFFLAGS). Each test then has its own loopback and its own port space, so any number of servers may bind 11729, 4104, 1729 and 8000 at once. The gate keeps the whole workspace, keeps nextest's parallelism, and needs no scope rule, no serial test group and no accepted red.
entries.resolved_by: implementation, 2026-08-21 — no owner choice was needed, because no coverage, policy or guarantee was traded away. An owner decision remains required for anything that would REDUCE what the gate covers; see OD-018 for the one cost this leaves on the table.

measured.before: cargo nextest run --manifest-path fork/typedb/Cargo.toml --workspace --all-features --no-fail-fast: 711 tests, 655 passed, 56 FAILED across 10 binaries. (The '3 failures' in the original default_in_force was itself an artefact: nextest had cancelled the run.)
measured.with_isolation_only: 711 tests, 659 passed, 52 failed, ZERO 'Address already in use'. Every remaining failure was a missing runtime FIXTURE, not a port: 49 behaviour targets reading Cucumber features through a Bazel-equivalent runfiles link cargo does not create, and 3 assembly-family targets needing the packaged server in their working directory.
measured.with_isolation_and_fixtures: 711 tests, 711 passed, 1 skipped (upstream's own #[ignore] in storage/tests/test_isolation.rs, TODO typedb#7033), exit 0, 1215 s. Re-measured THROUGH the controller: `cargo xtask quality fast` reports rust.tests pass, 1929 s.
measured.side_effect: typedb_server_bin::test_fail_points::test_fail_point_always, which the U0 lane recorded as FAILED after 1753 s with 'Could not serve HTTP on 0.0.0.0:8000: Address already in use', PASSES under isolation in 599 s. The lane runner already executes one target at a time, so that failure was a collision with something else on the machine — a class of false red isolation removes from the LANES too, not only from the gate.

entries.why_safe: The scheme cannot fail silently. netns_exec.py NEVER falls back to running unisolated: if the namespace cannot be created it exits 79 with the reason. The controller refuses in the same direction — before running any command that carries a _RUNNER variable it probes whether this machine can actually give out namespaces, and reports InfrastructureFailure rather than run without them. A machine that cannot isolate therefore gets 'this gate did not run', never a red that looks like a defect. The property the whole scheme rests on is regression-tested directly: exec::tests::two_isolated_processes_can_hold_the_same_port asserts that two processes bind 11729 simultaneously.
entries.why_structural: It keeps working when upstream adds another server test, which is exactly what a hand-maintained list of serial tests would not. Nothing names a port, a test or a binary.

entries.title: Should the fork's 711-test corpus run in the INNER loop, or only in `pr` and `full`?
entries.question: rust.tests is tier A, so `cargo xtask quality fast` runs the whole fork corpus on every invocation. Measured 2026-08-21: 1215 s standalone, 1929 s inside a controller run whose clippy pass preceded it — roughly 20-32 minutes of wall clock for a change that may not touch fork/ at all. Should the corpus stay unconditional, or become diff-conditional in `fast`?
entries.default_in_force: It runs, unconditionally, in every mode. Maximum coverage, maximum wall clock. Nothing is hidden and no result is weakened; the cost is paid by whoever runs the inner loop.
entries.why_safe: Over-running a gate can only cost time; under-running one can cost a regression. The safe default is therefore the expensive one. It is not obviously CORRECT: the same function already makes the TypeScript and Python gates diff-conditional in `fast` for exactly this reason, and fork/typedb's only path dependency outside its own tree is sources/slatedb-fork, which is materialised from source-lock rather than authored here — so a diff touching only tools/ or control-plane/ cannot change what the corpus does.
entries.owner_decision_changes: gates::targets() would narrow rust_manifests_all for `fast` to workspaces the diff can affect (fork/**, source-lock/**, the toolchain pin), leaving `pr` and `full` unchanged. That is a change to gate SELECTION, which is protected policy, and it trades a small real risk (a change that affects the fork through a route not modelled here) for ~20 minutes per inner loop. The implementation must not make that trade on its own.
entries.decision: Option B. The fork corpus becomes diff-conditional in `fast` ALONE: it is skipped only when every changed path is documentation or control-plane — a list of what is provably INERT, not a list of what is relevant, so an unmodelled route runs the corpus rather than skipping it. `tools/**` is deliberately NOT inert: `rust.tests` runs an overlay through tools/dev/netns_exec.py and stages its fixtures with tools/catalog/stage_test_fixtures.py, so a change there changes the run. An EMPTY change set is not inert either — `fast` with no diff is the ‘verify this tree’ run and has nothing to prove irrelevant. `pr`, the merge gate, and `full` are unchanged and still execute every workspace.
entries.why_this_is_not_a_loophole: It is the rule gates::targets() already applies to the TypeScript and Python gates, for the same reason. fork/typedb's only path dependency outside its own tree is sources/slatedb-fork, which is materialised from source-lock rather than authored here. Nothing can reach the default branch on the strength of a skip: `pr` runs the corpus unconditionally. The skip is also STATED in the gate's own pass detail, never silent — a skipped workspace that goes unmentioned reads as a workspace that passed.

entries.title: Protected-path disclosure: two disk guards inside the quality controller were LOOSENED
entries.question: Round 7d modified xtask/src/quality/{exec,gates}.rs, which `xtask/**` protects. Most of that diff adds capability or refusals, but two changes RELAX a guard. Are both relaxations accepted?
relaxations: (1) The per-workspace disk floor is no longer charged to a command that compiles nothing. `Cmd` gained `builds`, derived from `is_cargo_invocation` and lowered explicitly only by `.already_built()`. Before: every command of a heavy gate was charged the workspace floor. After: `rust.tests`'s staging step and its test RUN are charged the light floor (0.5 GB), because the build that precedes them in the same gate has already spent and met that floor.

(2) The gate-level cost-class floor now applies to INTERNAL gates only. Before: every gate was charged its class floor (12 GB heavy) before any command ran, AND each command was charged again. After: gates with commands are charged per command, which knows the workspace and whether the command builds; internal gates, which run no commands, keep the class check.
entries.default_in_force: Both relaxations are IN EFFECT in the merged tree, because without them `rust.tests` on the fork workspace cannot run at all on the 37 GB machine this project is required to work on: measured 2026-08-21, the build leaves 9.4 GB free and the run was then refused for wanting 16 GB — the space its own build had just spent.
entries.why_safe: Neither changes what a gate CONCLUDES, only whether it is attempted. The purpose of the floor is to stop an ENOSPC mid-compile being mistaken for a tool bug; a command that compiles nothing cannot produce that failure, and if the disk does run out anyway ENOSPC is typed InfrastructureFailure, so being wrong here fails safe — a refused run, never a false pass. The cold-tree build floor (16 GB for rust.tests@fork/typedb/Cargo.toml) is UNCHANGED and was met with roughly 0.2 GB to spare in the verifying run.
entries.not_self_approved: The implementation did NOT record an owner approval for this, unlike OD-012 where one was given explicitly. It is disclosed here so the loosening is visible in the register rather than absorbed into a large diff. Every other change in that diff adds a refusal or a capability and takes nothing away.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Accepting closes this entry. Rejecting means `rust.tests` cannot cover the fork workspace on a machine of this size, which returns the repository to the choice OD-017 was raised for.
entries.decision: Option A: both relaxations ACCEPTED as they stand, with no further change. The per-workspace build floor is not charged to a command that compiles nothing, and the gate-level cost-class floor applies to internal gates only.
entries.residual: A non-building command keeps the light floor (0.5 GB), which is a number chosen for gates that parse source files rather than for a test run that extracts three ~250 MB archives and writes RocksDB data (measured consumption ~0.6-1 GB). Declining to replace it with a measured scratch floor is safe because the failure mode is ENOSPC, which is typed InfrastructureFailure: being wrong costs a wasted run, never a wrong verdict.

entries.title: How strict is this repository's Python type checking?
entries.question: `py.typecheck` runs `basedpyright tools`. The repository had no type-checker config at all, so the tool's own default applied and the tier-A gate could not pass. A level had to be declared for the gate to mean anything. Which level is the repository's?
entries.default_in_force: pyrightconfig.json declares typeCheckingMode "standard" — pyright's own documented default — and all 86 findings at that level are FIXED, so the gate passes on merit rather than on a lowered bar.

measured.what the 86 were: 43 None-safety (Optional subscript / member access / iterable), 23 argument-type and attribute-access, and the rest single instances. Every one was a real path: a bazel query rule with no name attribute, tarfile.extractfile returning None for a non-regular member while the release digest hashed it anyway, `server.proc.returncode` read on a server that failed to start, a differential side with no bundles reporting "0 regressions", the ed25519 base point's x coordinate used without checking it exists.
measured.cost of the higher bar: Of the 373, roughly 201 are annotation and idiom work that cannot hide a defect — reportMissingTypeArgument (106: `dict` instead of `dict[str, int]`) and reportAttributeAccessIssue (95: attributes set dynamically on module objects). The other ~164 CAN hide one: reportArgumentType (71), reportIndexIssue (41), reportOptionalMemberAccess (15), reportCallIssue (15), reportOperatorIssue (11), reportGeneralTypeIssues (11). That second group is the same family that produced 7 real defects out of the 69 findings fixed at "standard".
measured.\"recommended\" with the same executionE: 373 errors, 12683 warnings. MEASURED 2026-08-21, superseding the 429 first quoted here: that figure was extrapolated from a run whose imports did not resolve, so it counted findings that correct execution environments remove.

entries.why_safe: "standard" is a real bar, not a formality: it caught 86 findings that a passing tier-A gate had been hiding behind an InfrastructureFailure. Declaring it makes the gate's meaning explicit and auditable; leaving it undeclared meant the level was whatever version of basedpyright happened to be installed, which is not a policy at all.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Either raise typeCheckingMode to "recommended" and pay all 373, or keep "standard" and turn on only the ~164 rules that can hide a defect while leaving the ~201 annotation rules off. Nothing else moves: the gate command, the tier and the failure semantics are unchanged either way.
entries.decision: Option C. typeCheckingMode stays "standard", and the strict rules that CAN hide a defect are enabled individually on top of it. The ~201 findings that are annotation and idiom work (reportMissingTypeArgument, reportAttributeAccessIssue) stay off: `dict` instead of `dict[str, int]` cannot make a verifier accept a forgery.
entries.expected_yield: The 69 findings fixed at "standard" produced 7 genuine defects — roughly one in ten, and of the kind that matters here (release.py hashing a None payload so an artifact digest could match an archive MISSING a file; leaf_diff.py reporting ‘0 regressions’ over an empty intersection). The rules enabled here are the same family. The rate will be lower on the marginal rules — the "standard" set is the one most correlated with runtime failure — so the yield is expected to be smaller than one in ten, not larger.

entries.title: 84 cucumber rows upstream's own runner never executes
entries.question: 84 plan rows name scenarios that carry `@ignore` (69, native runner) or `@ignore-typedb-http` (15, http runner). Upstream's runners filter those out by their own `is_ignore` predicate, so they are never executed and have no outcome to record. Are they a declared exclusion, or do they stay in the denominator as permanently uncovered?
entries.default_in_force: They stay in the denominator and are reported UNCOVERED, with the reason naming the exact tag and the runner that filters it — leaf_coverage.py's `uncovered_reasons` already distinguishes them from 'no evidence' rows, so nothing is hidden today.
entries.why_safe: Counting them as covered would be a lie about 84 scenarios nobody ran. Reporting them as UNCOVERED-with-a-reason is true and visible. It is not CORRECT, though, in the sense that it leaves 84 rows permanently short of a ceiling nobody can reach: no amount of execution moves them while upstream's filter stands, so a coverage number that includes them understates by a fixed amount forever.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Declaring them out of scope the way OD-010 declared the cluster suites: they would be enumerated, reported as a declared exclusion with this rationale, and removed from the denominator rather than from the report. The alternative is to keep them and accept that the ceiling is 84 rows lower than it looks.

entries.title: 132 FAILPOINT rows at a granularity upstream does not emit
entries.question: The catalogue enumerates 44 FAILPOINT leaves per profile (132 across U0/U1/U2) from the `fail_points!` macro. Upstream tests them with TWO libtest cases — `test_fail_point_always` and `test_fail_point_chance` — each looping over every fail point internally. There is no per-fail-point outcome to record. Does the denominator keep the per-point granularity?
entries.default_in_force: The rows stay, reported PARTIAL for one profile (44) and UNCOVERED for the rest (88): target-granularity evidence exists and is recorded as such, and a leaf-granularity outcome does not, so no row is claimed covered.
entries.why_safe: PARTIAL is the honest status for evidence that a binary ran without a per-case outcome; it is the same treatment every zero-leaf cargo target gets. Both fail-point tests DO pass under the isolated runner (measured 2026-08-21: always 599 s, chance 965 s, both PASSED), so the property is exercised — what is missing is the per-point attribution, not the testing.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Either the denominator drops to 2 FAILPOINT leaves per profile, matching what upstream emits (the catalogue generator would enumerate the libtest cases rather than the macro's members), or an upstream change makes each fail point its own case. The first is a catalogue change and shrinks a denominator, which is exactly the move this project refuses to make without a recorded decision.

entries.title: The one SCRIPT row: a crash loop with no assertion, and no Bazel referent
entries.question: `shell:tool/test/simulate-crash.sh::crash-restart-loop` is the plan's only SCRIPT row. Should a lane execute it?
entries.default_in_force: It is UNCOVERED, and this round deliberately did NOT produce evidence for it while building the STATIC_CHECK lane beside it.
entries.why_safe: Executing it would produce a green that means nothing, which is worse than an honest gap. Read the script: it loops `docker run bazel:assemble-linux-x86_64`, sleeps, kills the container, and `exit 0`s on a 600-second timeout REGARDLESS of what happened. It asserts nothing and cannot fail. It also needs a Bazel-BUILT docker image (analysis alone is not enough) and a docker daemon, and `tools/bazel/bazel_parity.py` already records `//tool/test:simulate-crash` as a catalogue entry with NO Bazel referent at the pinned revision — a real catalogue defect, kept rather than deleted because deleting a plan row silently is how a denominator shrinks.
entries.owner_decision_changes: Either the row is a declared exclusion (the target does not exist upstream at the pin), or someone writes a crash-recovery test that actually asserts recovery — which is product work with a real specification behind it, not a port of this script.

entries.title: The Rust fuzz campaign: build it, or narrow the claim
entries.question: `quality full` and the nightly/release workflows describe a long libFuzzer campaign. No production workspace has a `fuzz/` directory, so no such campaign has ever run. Does the owner want the campaign BUILT (cargo-fuzz targets over the authored surfaces), or the documented claim NARROWED to say the project does not fuzz yet?
entries.safe_default: R8-P0-05: the gate now reports INFRASTRUCTURE naming .quality/campaigns.toml, so `full` can neither pass on the campaign nor emit a red verdict about code that was never fuzzed. Full therefore cannot be green while this decision is open, which is the correct posture: the audit's rule is that a placeholder must not satisfy a workflow claim that the campaign ran.
entries.why_safe_not_correct: It is safe because it cannot overstate anything, and it is not correct because the surfaces that most deserve fuzzing are exactly the ones round 8 found defects in: the object-store key-class grammar, the recovery record and checkpoint-metadata parsers, the backend-identity marker, the object digest framing and capability canonicalisation. .quality/campaigns.toml names them so the eventual work is scoped rather than invented.
entries.what_a_decision_would_change: BUILD: add a `fuzz/` workspace with libFuzzer targets for the named surfaces, set implemented = true, and give the campaign a time budget and a corpus/crash artefact bound to the commit and the tool version. NARROW: record the narrowing here, remove the campaign's claim from the nightly and release workflow prose, and mark the gate advisory — which is a policy change, not a controller default.

entries.title: Upstream's 16 dependency advisories: carry them, or fork the lockfile
entries.question: The materialised TypeDB fork's transitive graph carries 16 RUSTSEC advisories at the pinned revision - 9 vulnerabilities/unsound and 7 unmaintained crates. None was selected by this project, and none can be fixed without re-resolving upstream's Cargo.lock. Does the owner want them CARRIED (the fork stays byte-identical to the pinned upstream revision, and the qualification corpus keeps measuring that exact tree), or the LOCKFILE FORKED (bump h2, rustls-webpki, quick-xml, remove_dir_all and replace tempdir, then re-run every lane against the new tree)?
entries.safe_default: R8-P1-05: each advisory is listed INDIVIDUALLY in fork/typedb/deny.toml with its reason, so the gate passes on exactly this set and fails on any addition. A NEW advisory, or one on a crate this project introduces, is a real red.
entries.why_safe_not_correct: It is safe because the set is enumerated and cannot grow silently, and because the reachability of most of them here is nil: the rustls-webpki and rustls-pemfile findings are on a TLS path no lane exercises (no cluster, no certificates), quick-xml parses no attacker-supplied XML, pprof is a profiling dependency no gate enables, and remove_dir_all is reached only through tempdir in a dev-dependency. It is not correct because h2 IS on the server's request path, and because 'upstream will fix it' is not a schedule.
entries.what_a_decision_would_change: CARRY: the entries stay, with review dates, and a G2 run states them in its risk record. FORK THE LOCK: fork/typedb/Cargo.lock diverges from the pinned upstream revision, which changes the executed-tree identity every sealed leaf bundle is bound to - so every lane is re-run and every bundle re-sealed. That is a deliberate, expensive choice, which is why it is the owner's.

entries.title: Pre-auth rate limiting on the managed Worker: which mechanism, and what budget
entries.question: R8-P2-04 requires that every unauthenticated or pre-auth surface be rate-limited as well as body-capped. The body cap is implemented and tested (MAX_REQUEST_BODY_BYTES / MAX_STRUCTURAL_BODY_BYTES in control-plane/src/controller/worker-entry.ts, with REQUEST_BODY_TOO_LARGE refusals proved by executed tests). Rate limiting is not, and it cannot be chosen here: a per-isolate token bucket is not a rate limit across a Cloudflare deployment, Cloudflare's native rate-limiting binding needs an account-level budget the owner sets, and WAF rate-limiting rules live outside this repository entirely. Which mechanism, and at what requests-per-period budget per client, for the pre-auth surfaces (/live, /ready, /health and the capability frame check that precedes any Durable Object contact)?
entries.safe_default: There is no public route today and the posture that removes one is machine-checked: wrangler.toml sets workers_dev = false and preview_urls = false, and stack/wrangler-check.mjs FAILS pre-deployment if either is anything but explicitly false, in both the config and the canonical graph. With no workers.dev URL, no preview URL and no declared route, there is no unauthenticated surface for an anonymous client to reach, so the absent rate limit currently guards a door that is not open.
entries.why_safe_not_correct: Safe only while that stays true. The first `[[routes]]` entry, or the first service that fronts this Worker, makes the pre-auth surfaces reachable and the rate limit load-bearing on the same day — and a default of 'none' is then indistinguishable from an oversight. It is also the wrong PLACE to be safe: the protection this project actually wants in front of a public route is an outer service identity (Cloudflare Access or mTLS), with the capability still required underneath, and a rate limit is the floor beneath that, not a substitute for it.
entries.what_a_decision_would_change: NATIVE BINDING: a rate-limiting binding is declared in wrangler.toml and in stack/graph.data.mjs, worker-entry.ts consults it before any pre-auth work, and the managed profile REFUSES to serve when the binding is absent (fail closed, like every other managed input). WAF RULE: the budget lives outside this repository, and the posture check gains an attestation field naming the rule so the gap is recorded rather than assumed. EITHER WAY the route-posture check below becomes enforceable: a declared route with no declared outer identity and no declared limiter fails pre-deployment.
